081.title: A mushroom, before and after the cut
081.caption: The reference shows an intact bolete on the forest floor. The recording holds on cut faces, then switches to a different arrangement on a board. The strongest sampled visual jump lands at six seconds.
081.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 2:30 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
081.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Mean absolute BT.601 luma difference between adjacent 4-Hz frames at 96 × 64. Times label the later frame.

050.title: The cost of starting every subtitle clock at zero
050.caption: For 10,544 of 45,333 nonzero-start rows, reading the recording’s opening ten seconds reverses the answer to “does this clip contain a cue onset?”
050.scope: 45,333 sampled rows with nonzero source offsets · paired clock comparison
050.method: Compare [stored start, stored start + 10) against [0,10) on the very same subtitle track. Agreement on presence alone can still retrieve completely different text.

002.title: When an image has two recordings
002.caption: Both recordings supply ten windows for 14,674 WIT entries. The other populated cells show how differently two recordings can be sampled.
002.scope: 37,706 two-recording WIT entries · one observation per pair
002.method: Restrict to WIT indices with exactly two recording IDs. Sort the pair by increasing number of rows. Cells below the diagonal are impossible.

092.title: A dragonfly beside a reef aquarium
092.caption: The linked WIT image is a dragonfly. The video frames show coral under blue aquarium lighting. Only a small fraction of their coarse colour histograms overlaps.
092.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 3:30 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
092.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. The five most frequent bins in each 64-bin RGB histogram, displayed at bin-centre colours with widths proportional to pixel share within the five shown. The printed overlap uses all 64 bins.

063.title: Where in the frame do pixels change?
063.caption: The middle half of the frame by width and height holds 31.8% of the change on average. That rectangle occupies 25% of the picture.
063.scope: 200 clips with nonzero sampled frame change · equal clip weight
063.method: Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Compute absolute luma differences of adjacent frames. Sum on an 8 × 12 grid, normalise each nonzero clip to 100%, then average the maps. The outline marks the central quarter of the image.

086.title: The ingredient and the cooking operation
086.caption: The reference caption describes raw tenderloin. The video shows browned meat being basted and turned. No new subtitle starts in these ten seconds, although the audio track carries energy.
086.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:30 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
086.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Each point measures mono 16-kHz audio RMS in a 100-ms bin. Level does not identify the sound source.

074.title: Do louder seconds also change more visibly?
074.caption: Median within-clip correlation is +0.03 on the original clock and -0.08 after rotating sound by five seconds. Individual recordings cover a wide range.
074.scope: 200 clips with nonconstant sound and frame-change profiles
074.method: Pearson correlation across ten paired one-second bins per nonconstant clip. The comparison rotates the audio bins cyclically by five seconds. A descriptive alignment check with no significance test.

093.title: Three geographies in one electoral record
093.caption: The WIT caption locates a district in Greater Adelaide. The recording title asks about Canadian electoral districts. The diagram inside the clip labels Texas. All three are visible clues to the link’s meaning.
093.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
093.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Mean absolute BT.601 luma difference between adjacent 4-Hz frames at 96 × 64. Times label the later frame.

020.title: Eight real timelines with ten ticks each
020.caption: The first and last timelines have the same number of rows. Their first-to-last spans are 4.5 and 81 minutes.
020.scope: Eight source timelines selected by span rank from 88,075 ten-window recordings
020.method: Select the observed recording at each stated quantile rank of span, breaking ties by recording ID. Ticks show all ten stored starts relative to the first. Record links open the first row.

096.title: The geometry that disappears on black
096.caption: The WIT diagram stores dark lines on transparency. A white background reveals the construction. The linked recording has its own drawn geometry and a title about Miquel’s theorem.
096.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
096.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Composite the original orientation-corrected PNG over white and black. Count fully transparent (alpha 0) and fully opaque (alpha 255) pixels.

038.title: Do search orderings agree at the top?
038.caption: The first result agrees for 22 of 62 paired queries. The top-five lists have mean overlap 34.4% by intersection over union.
038.scope: Historical collector snapshot · 62 queries with both saved search orderings
038.method: Truncate each saved list to its first k available IDs. Compare sets with Jaccard overlap, then average equally over paired queries. Lists shorter than k use all available IDs.

098.title: Habitat first, toadlet later
098.caption: The reference shows the dark underside of a toadlet. The clip moves from vegetation to a bright orange animal. The colour maps locate the orange pixels, and both subtitle starts arrive after nine seconds.
098.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
098.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Decode RGB frames at 4 Hz, 96 × 64. Class a pixel as orange when R ≥ 100, R ≥ 1.25G, G ≥ 1.35B and R − B ≥ 55. Each map cell shows the fraction of 64 pixels that pass. The same colour threshold applies to the animal and its surroundings. Dashed lines mark subtitle onsets.

090.title: A whole rail route and one passing train
090.caption: A red line on a map stands for the route. The recording shows platform furniture and then a train coming into view. Its first stored subtitle cue arrives after eight seconds.
090.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
090.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Tick marks show nonempty subtitle onsets within [source offset, source offset + 10 s). Cue ends are unknown.

046.title: What does the subtitle say beyond the title?
046.caption: In 18,482 word-bearing windows every distinct subtitle word is absent from the recording title. The median window adds 20 distinct word types.
046.scope: 41,422 ten-second windows with subtitle word tokens
046.method: Join cue texts whose starts fall in the first ten seconds. Compare distinct case-folded Unicode word types with those of the recording title. Word difference measures vocabulary, not semantic novelty.

078.title: Is the linked picture closer in colour?
078.caption: Median palette overlap is 42.1% for the linked WIT image and 40.2% across other pairings in this panel. Colour alone cannot identify a subject.
078.scope: 200 linked pairs and 39,800 off-diagonal reference-image/clip pairs
078.method: Reference images use white behind transparency. Colour histograms use four bins per R, G and B channel at 96 × 64 pixels. Histogram intersection sums the smaller proportion in each bin. Compare the original diagonal to all off-diagonal pairs. Other pairings can share content or colour; they are a descriptive reference.

034.title: Which title themes accumulate more windows?
034.caption: A matched craft and repair recording contributes 8.82 rows on average. The corresponding mean for health and medicine is 7.46.
034.scope: Complete release · recording-title keyword hits · one mean per vocabulary list
034.method: Divide matching release rows by distinct matching recording IDs within each fixed English title vocabulary. Sources can occur under more than one theme.

099.title: A neighbourhood outside and a home inside
099.caption: The reference caption places subdivision houses behind a rice field. The recording travels through a furnished interior. Its soundtrack has measurable energy even without a new subtitle onset.
099.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 2:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
099.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Each point measures mono 16-kHz audio RMS in a 100-ms bin. Level does not identify the sound source.

079.title: How much clip remains after the first ten seconds?
079.caption: All 28,969 eligible clips support the original ten-second window. 1,162 have a stored duration below 20 seconds, limiting a second nonoverlapping window.
079.scope: 28,969 eligible recordings from a 30,000-component candidate draw · first ten seconds
079.method: Count original eligible rows with recorded container duration at least each threshold. Thresholds overlap. Container duration alone cannot verify precise decoded coverage at the boundary.

011.title: Where does the retained timeline start and end?
011.caption: 79.0% of recordings include the source opening. The last retained start is at least ten minutes in for 29.9%.
011.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
011.method: Compare empirical cumulative distributions of minimum and maximum clip-start offsets by recording. The last retained start is a lower bound on source length.

055.title: Which frequencies get heard in an average?
055.caption: The lowest band contributes 34.6% when each nonzero clip gets one vote and 40.7% when spectral power is pooled across clips.
055.scope: 200 clips with nonzero spectral power · six frequency bands
055.method: Average power from four 25-ms Hann-windowed real FFTs per 100 ms. Sum frequency-bin power within bands. Equal-clip weighting normalises within each nonzero clip.

067.title: A detailed picture can sit perfectly still
067.caption: 47 clips have above-median spatial contrast and below-median temporal change. A busy frame has two different meanings here.
067.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
067.method: Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Spatial contrast is the standard deviation of luma within a frame, averaged across the clip. Temporal change is the mean absolute difference between adjacent sampled frames.

001.title: Which recordings does a random row favour?
001.caption: Ten-window recordings make up 61.5% of recording IDs. They supply 75.1% of the rows a row sampler would see.
001.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
001.method: Count each recording ID once, then weight that same histogram by its number of stored rows.

003.title: Does one sibling dominate the link?
003.caption: In 2,717 pairs, one recording supplies over four fifths of the linked rows. A row sampler gives those siblings very different exposure.
003.scope: 37,706 paired WIT entries · share of rows from the more sampled recording
003.method: For each two-recording WIT entry, divide the larger row count by the sum for the pair.

004.title: Where do the rows concentrate?
004.caption: The largest connected group contains 159,887 rows. The top 1% of groups account for 18.0% of the release.
004.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
004.method: Rank units from largest to smallest separately. A connected group links rows transitively through a shared recording ID, WIT index or stored Wikipedia page URL. A group can cover many distinct subjects.

005.title: What changes when a group gets one vote?
005.caption: Groups over 1,000 rows supply 13.6% of all rows, although only 1 of 80,187 groups reaches that size.
005.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
005.method: For each size bracket, divide the number of groups by all groups and the number of rows they contain by all rows. Both rows of the plot sum to 100%.

006.title: Which identities cross release splits?
006.caption: Recording IDs stay in one original split. 777 WIT entries span two, and 70 connected groups reach all three.
006.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
006.method: Count the number of distinct original split labels per unit. Connected groups are transitive metadata relationships. Counts do not establish duplicated media.

007.title: What does opening one shard buy?
007.caption: A typical test shard has 6,139 rows, compared with 1,755 in training. Choosing a file uniformly changes how often a row can appear.
007.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
007.method: Compute row counts separately for every release shard, then take the median within each original split. File counts accompany the labels.

008.title: Where do rows go after grouping?
008.caption: 235,258 original training rows enter the grouped test partition. The grouped partition keeps connected records together.
008.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
008.method: Rows are counted at the intersection of original release label and the recorded experimental component assignment, before eligibility or balanced sample selection.

009.title: Which recordings straddle a file boundary?
009.caption: 537 recording IDs have rows in two shards. Reading one shard can leave part of their timeline elsewhere in the release.
009.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
009.method: Count distinct source shards for each recording ID and tally IDs spanning multiple shards, grouped by the number of stored windows.

010.title: How often would two random rows meet?
010.caption: Per million pairs of distinct rows, about 6.9 share a recording ID and 18,616 share a connected group. The large group drives much of the difference.
010.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
010.method: Exact finite-population probability: sum n(n−1) over units divided by N(N−1), for two rows drawn uniformly without replacement. Relationships are nested; bars do not add.

012.title: How far is the next retained moment?
012.caption: 63.2% of adjacent starts are 30 seconds apart. 5,894 neighbouring pairs are separated by more than 15 minutes.
012.method: Sort distinct starts within each recording ID and difference adjacent offsets, counting each within-recording transition once.

013.title: How long do consecutive 30-second runs last?
013.caption: 288,906 starts have no immediate 30-second neighbour on either side. 7,018 complete runs reach ten consecutive positions.
013.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
013.method: Start a new run at the start of each recording and whenever adjacent recorded offsets differ from 30 seconds. Count maximal runs at each length.

014.title: Ten clips can occupy very different spans
014.caption: Among recordings with ten retained starts, the middle 80% reach their last start between 5.0 and 26.0 minutes after the first.
014.scope: 88,075 recordings with exactly ten retained starts
014.method: Align each ten-start recording to its first retained moment. At each ordinal position take the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles across recordings.

015.title: How far apart are the ends of a collection?
015.caption: The median first-to-last span grows from 0.5 minutes for two-window sources to 9.0 for ten-window sources.
015.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
015.method: For each recording, subtract the first retained start from the last. Quantiles include all recordings of the indicated depth.

016.title: The largest jump inside each recording
016.caption: 1,052 recordings contain an internal gap of at least half an hour. Their other stored starts may lie close together.
016.scope: 140,815 multi-window recordings · each recording counted once per threshold
016.method: Keep only the largest gap per recording with at least two rows. Threshold counts are cumulative.

017.title: How many time slots are empty between the ends?
017.caption: 59,757 sources fill every 30-second slot between their first and last stored starts. In 13,990, less than a quarter of that grid is occupied.
017.scope: 140,815 recordings with at least two distinct starts
017.method: All release starts are multiples of 30 s. Divide distinct retained starts by 1 + (last−first)/30. This concerns the internal grid only.

018.title: How different are two timelines for one image?
018.caption: In 8,748 WIT pairs the longer timeline covers at least five times as many 30-second slots as the shorter one.
018.scope: 37,706 WIT indices linked to two distinct recording IDs
018.method: For the two recording IDs of each WIT, count all grid positions between first and last retained starts inclusive. Divide the larger size by the smaller.

019.title: Which recordings keep their opening?
019.caption: Of 55,175 recordings with fewer than ten windows, 1 misses time zero. Among ten-window recordings, 65.8% retain the opening.
019.scope: Complete release · 1,172,262 rows · 143,250 recording IDs · 105,544 WIT indices
019.method: Group recordings by number of stored starts and measure the fraction whose earliest retained offset equals zero.

021.title: Which Wikipedia editions travel together?
021.caption: Among entries with Portuguese metadata, 57.9% also carry Spanish metadata. Reading across a row holds its first edition fixed.
021.scope: 105,544 WIT entries · first stored row per WIT ID in sorted shard and row order
021.method: Use distinct language codes in one representative per WIT ID. Display the eight most frequent codes other than English. Each cell is a conditional percentage.

022.title: Does another edition bring a fuller English record?
022.caption: English alt text appears in 8.1% of single-edition entries and 26.3% of entries with nine or more editions.
022.scope: 105,544 WIT entries · first stored row per WIT ID in sorted shard and row order
022.method: Group WIT representatives by distinct code count. Count fields containing at least one Unicode word token across the English slots in each row.

023.title: One language code can occupy several slots
023.caption: 27,141 WIT representatives list English more than once. Keeping just the first English slot can discard another description.
023.scope: 105,544 WIT entries · first stored row per WIT ID in sorted shard and row order
023.method: For each displayed code, divide entries with two or more appearances by entries that carry that code. Other slot contents can repeat or differ.

024.title: Is the picture the page’s main image?
024.caption: Every observed flag is true across 105,198 WIT representatives. In this release slice the main-image flag cannot separate cover pictures from other illustrations.
024.scope: 105,544 WIT entries · first stored row per WIT ID in sorted shard and row order
024.method: Classify each representative using its available is_main_image booleans. 346 entries with no supplied flag are omitted.

025.title: How much text fits around one image?
025.caption: The median nonempty English reference caption has 8 words. Page context has 60.
025.scope: 105,544 WIT entries · first stored row per WIT ID in sorted shard and row order
025.method: Count Unicode alphanumeric tokens in distinct English strings concatenated within a field. Each field uses only WIT entries with a positive token count.

026.title: What can the section add to the page?
026.caption: In 11,957 entries every section-context word type also appears in the page context. In 14,107, at least three quarters occur only in the section context of the two fields.
026.scope: 57,694 WIT representatives with English page and section context
026.method: Compute the share of distinct case-folded section word types absent from English page context. Common words count; overlap is lexical.

027.title: Short article titles meet longer video titles
027.caption: 74,954 recording titles have at least six words while their linked English page title has five or fewer.
027.scope: 143,250 recording IDs · first stored row per recording in sorted shard and row order
027.method: Count Unicode word tokens in the recording title and joined distinct English page titles on its representative row. Count recording IDs in each size combination.

028.title: Where does a recording title echo?
028.caption: Page context contains at least half of the recording-title vocabulary for 30.2% of these sources. The shorter reference caption does so for 15.7%.
028.scope: 131,129 recordings with a page title, reference caption and page context
028.method: Case-fold Unicode word tokens and use distinct types. A type match includes common words. Keeping all three fields nonempty fixes the recording population; longer context offers more chances to match.

029.title: What else is inside a video description?
029.caption: 79,782 descriptions contain a web-address marker. 8,669 contain a clock-like timestamp, a possible lead for navigating a source recording.
029.method: Search the stored description for HTTP(S) or www, a hash followed by a word, and a digits:two-digits pattern. One description may match several. A timestamp match is not a verified chapter.

030.title: Two videos can share a picture and no title words
030.caption: 24,613 pairs share no title word at all. At the other extreme, 45 pairs have identical sets of title words.
030.scope: 37,706 WIT entries with two recording IDs · one title comparison per pair
030.method: Take the intersection over the union of the two case-folded recording-title vocabularies for each WIT entry with exactly two recording IDs. Common words are retained.

031.title: Which topics dominated the original annotation chart?
031.caption: Geography and Nature (24.5%) and People and Biographies (22.5%) together account for 47% of the chart’s assignments.
031.scope: Historical annotation charts · reported shares · original denominator unknown
031.method: Replot the rounded shares printed on the historical category chart. The annotated records and sampling denominator could not be recovered. These shares describe that chart.

032.title: What did the chart mean by geography?
032.caption: “Global” accounts for 25.1% of the historical assignments. The inclusion of Mars makes clear how far a topic association can be from a filming location.
032.scope: Historical annotation charts · reported shares · original denominator unknown
032.method: Replot all reported labels exactly from the historic geographic-association chart. They were attached to topics; geographic coordinates and filming places were never observed.

033.title: When do two titles name the same theme?
033.caption: Among rows matching land and water in either title, 26.8% match it in both. The rest announce the theme on just one side.
033.scope: All release rows · 11 fixed English keyword lists · denominator varies by theme
033.method: For each vocabulary list, partition matching rows by which titles contain a listed token. Categories overlap across themes. Exact vocabularies are in the data.

035.title: Which concept chapters find a page link?
035.caption: 37 of 56 animal entries have a candidate link. The denominator on each label shows how much the chapter was tested.
035.scope: 429 reference entries across 11 chapters · automated page matches to TALI
035.method: An entry is linked when its candidate entity has a matching page URL in the TALI metadata. Chapter rates depend on this particular reference inventory and unreviewed mappings.

036.title: How many windows stand behind a concept match?
036.caption: The elephant entry shown reaches 5 source recordings and 30 rows. Repeated windows amplify a concept’s apparent depth.
036.scope: Seven named candidate links · counts of WIT entries, recording IDs and release rows
036.method: For each illustrated English entity label choose the language entry with most linked recording IDs, then lexical language-code order. No audiovisual depiction has been certified.

037.title: Different reference languages can meet at one entity
037.caption: 79 candidate entities appear in more than one language list. Adding the lists together counts some of the same entity candidates twice.
037.scope: 425 reference entries with candidate Wikidata IDs · 301 distinct IDs
037.method: Group nonempty candidate Wikidata IDs by the number of distinct reference-language codes. Entity resolution remains automated.

039.title: Where does a high-ranked result go?
039.caption: Of 62 first-ranked relevance results, 34 fall outside the other ordering’s top five. The diagonal shows how often a result keeps its place.
039.scope: Historical collector snapshot · 62 queries with both saved search orderings
039.method: For each of the first five relevance results available, locate its ID in the saved view-count ordering. The final column includes absent IDs and positions below five.

040.title: Change the query or change the ordering?
040.caption: Median candidate overlap is 0% across query variants at fixed ordering and 44% across orderings at fixed query.
040.scope: Historical collector · 77 within-entry query pairs · 62 within-query ordering pairs
040.method: Compare full saved candidate sets by Jaccard overlap. All pairs of query variants in the same WIT entry and ordering contribute. These are different descriptive pair populations in a debug snapshot.

041.title: An empty window can have a busy parent track
041.caption: Of 8,788 windows without a cue onset in ten seconds, 8,197 have nonempty cues elsewhere in the same track.
041.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
041.method: Parse nonempty subtitle starts on the source clock. Assign each row to one of three mutually exclusive states. A subtitle already in progress can cross the left boundary.

042.title: What does waiting one more second buy?
042.caption: A five-second look finds a cue onset in 75.5% of rows. Extending it to 30 seconds picks up 7,812 more rows.
042.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
042.method: Count rows whose first nonempty cue starts strictly before the indicated right endpoint, including starts exactly at the left endpoint. All 30 durations use the same row set.

043.title: How many text updates fit inside the clip?
043.caption: The median row contains 3 nonempty cue starts in ten seconds and 10 in thirty. Some remain empty for both durations.
043.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
043.method: Count cue starts at offsets in [0,10) and [0,30) relative to each retained start. Count rows in mutually exclusive brackets.

044.title: Does cue availability persist within a recording?
044.caption: 3,198 recordings have an onset in every sampled ten-second window; 2,714 switch between covered and uncovered windows.
044.scope: 6,144 hash-selected recording IDs · all their stored rows
044.method: For every sampled recording, examine all its stored starts and count the share with a nonempty onset within ten seconds. A recording contributes once.

045.title: How close was the preceding subtitle?
045.caption: In 1,052 rows with no new onset in ten seconds, a cue had started within the preceding three seconds. Its end is unknown.
045.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
045.method: Measure distance to the last nonempty onset strictly before the row start. Use all rows in each named group as denominator, including rows without a preceding onset.

047.title: When a subtitle line echoes its predecessor
047.caption: 332 ten-second windows contain a verbatim repeat of the immediately preceding cue text. The one-cue windows have the highest repeat rate among the six counts shown.
047.scope: 41,422 ten-second windows with at least one cue onset
047.method: Compare trimmed, case-folded text at each onset to the preceding cue on its source track, even if the predecessor falls before the window. The chart shows the six common exact cue counts.

048.title: Does a fast subtitle track use shorter lines?
048.caption: In windows with two starts, the first line averages 8.6 words; with seven starts it averages 6.3. More updates need not mean proportionally more text.
048.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
048.method: Separate the first cue from later cues in a ten-second window. Compute mean Unicode word count per first cue and per later cue within each exact cue-count group. Show counts two through seven.

049.title: Subtitle density across the recording clock
049.caption: In the first five seconds, the earliest retained row averages 1.32 cue starts. The sixth and later retained rows average 1.48.
049.scope: 50,210 retained rows from 6,144 recordings · 2,048 recording IDs per original split
049.method: Sort retained starts within each sampled recording. Count cue starts per five-second bin and divide by all rows at the indicated ordinal positions, including empty windows.

051.title: A ten-second listening map
051.caption: The median ten-second RMS is 0.099 of digital full scale. The bright and dark streaks show how levels vary inside recordings with similar overall loudness.
051.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
051.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Display RMS in dB relative to full scale; colour saturates below −60 dB and above 0 dB. Rows sorted by whole-clip RMS.

052.title: How wide is the soundtrack’s dynamic range?
052.caption: The median clip spans 15.8 dB between its quieter and louder tenths. 25 clips span at least 30 dB.
052.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
052.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Compute each clip’s 90th minus 10th percentile level in dBFS. Bins below −100 dBFS are floored before subtraction.

053.title: How long does a quiet stretch last?
053.caption: At RMS below 0.01, 28 recordings sustain at least a second of quiet. At a 0.03 cutoff the count is 57.
053.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
053.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Find maximal consecutive runs strictly below each threshold; count clips reaching each duration. These thresholds describe level only.

054.title: A short peak can hide inside a quiet clip
054.caption: 69 decoded clips peak above nominal digital full scale. The plot preserves those floating-point samples; the whole-clip average is much lower.
054.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
054.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Use the largest absolute decoded sample and the RMS of all 160,000 mono samples. A floating-point peak above one alone does not prove source clipping.

056.title: Does the high-frequency share hold steady?
056.caption: At second one the middle half of clips place 1.2%–7.3% of their power above or at 2 kHz. Follow the band across the clip.
056.scope: 197 recordings with measurable spectral power in every second
056.method: Sum Hann-windowed FFT power over each consecutive second. Divide power at 2–8 kHz by total 0–8 kHz power. Omit clips with any all-zero second.

057.title: How much quiet would a window sampler see?
057.caption: 91 of 200 clips have no 100-ms bin below RMS 0.01. Across all recordings 1,948 of 20,000 bins fall below it.
057.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
057.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Add up bins below RMS 0.01 within each clip. Accumulated quiet can be spread across several intervals.

058.title: Can sign changes tell us about the spectrum?
058.caption: The correlation between sign-change rate and 2–8 kHz power share is 0.69 across these clips. The spread shows how differently the two measures behave.
058.method: Average the fraction of adjacent mono samples that cross zero within each 100-ms bin. Compare against whole-clip high-band power share; one point per nonzero clip.

059.title: How much energy fits in the loudest second?
059.caption: The ten loudest 100-ms bins carry a median 36.4% of the clip’s energy. They can come from different seconds of the recording.
059.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Sort bins by descending squared RMS within each nonzero clip, then plot cumulative energy fractions. The horizontal axis measures accumulated time after sorting.

060.title: Four recordings, four sound fingerprints
060.caption: Read each strip from left to right. The six rows separate low frequencies at the bottom from high frequencies at the top, following changes that a single RMS value merges.
060.scope: Four linked examples from the reserve panel · same ten-second clock
060.method: Each column is 100 ms. Six FFT-band powers are shown in dB relative to the loudest band-bin of that recording, floored at −50 dB. Normalisation is per recording.

061.title: How much does a square crop leave out?
061.caption: Only 4 of 200 stored WIT images are square. For the widest image an inscribed square would keep just 38.3% of its area.
061.scope: 200 verified WIT images · native dimensions before resizing
061.method: Use orientation-corrected source image dimensions. Ratios describe width divided by height. Hypothetical crop is a maximal inscribed square.

062.title: A ten-second map of light
062.caption: 17 clips include a sampled frame with mean luma below 10 on a 0–255 scale. Some dark bands are brief; others persist.
062.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
062.method: Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Horizontally adjacent cells are quarter-second frames. Sort rows by mean ten-second luma. Colour range is the full 0–255 scale.

064.title: When one frame transition carries the sequence
064.caption: For 8 clips, one quarter-second transition accounts for at least half the sampled pixel change.
064.scope: 200 clips with nonzero change · 39 transitions per clip
064.method: Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Divide the largest of 39 adjacent-frame mean absolute differences by their sum. Exact-zero sums are excluded. A large jump can reflect a cut, flash or camera movement.

065.title: One palette for a still, another for ten seconds
065.caption: The median reference uses 6.5 effective colour bins. Pooling the 40 video frames gives 8.0. The diagonal marks equal palette breadth.
065.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
065.method: Reference images use white behind transparency. Colour histograms use four bins per R, G and B channel at 96 × 64 pixels. Effective bins = exp(Shannon entropy in natural units). The video histogram pools all pixels across 40 frames; this also captures changes over time.

066.title: Does a bright reference lead to a bright video?
066.caption: The median absolute difference in mean luma is 36.5 levels across linked pairs. Both the image and clip are shown on the same 0–255 scale.
066.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
066.method: Reference images use white behind transparency. Colour histograms use four bins per R, G and B channel at 96 × 64 pixels. Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Compare one reference mean with the mean over forty video frames. A diagonal point has equal average brightness.

068.title: Do both sides lean toward the same colour?
068.caption: 88 pairs fall in the same red–blue balance band. 20 switch directly between blue-leaning and red-leaning.
068.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
068.method: Reference images use white behind transparency. Colour histograms use four bins per R, G and B channel at 96 × 64 pixels. Compute mean red minus mean blue. Values below −10 are blue-leaning, above +10 red-leaning, and the centre band includes both boundaries.

069.title: Which side has a broader light–dark range?
069.caption: 79 recordings have higher average per-frame tonal entropy than their linked reference image. Tonal variety can come from texture, labels or lighting.
069.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
069.method: Bin 8-bit luma into 16 equal-width levels; compute Shannon entropy in bits for the WIT image and separately for each sampled frame. Plot mean frame entropy minus WIT entropy; white matte for transparency.

070.title: A colour strip for every recording
070.caption: Each horizontal strip collapses 40 frames into 40 average colours. An abrupt stripe marks a large palette change; a textured but colour-stable scene can look uniform here.
070.scope: 200 media-eligible reserve recordings · first ten seconds of the stored clip
070.method: Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Each cell is the frame’s actual mean RGB, rounded down to 8 bits. Sort recordings by average red minus blue. Each strip spans ten seconds.

071.title: Do the sound and picture stay in the same state?
071.caption: 515 of 600 adjacent window pairs stay in the same state. Each switch below comes from the same ten-second recording.
071.scope: 200 media pairs · three within-recording transitions each · 600 transitions
071.method: Reuse the verified 800-window atlas measurements in original panel order. Four 2.5-s windows per clip; RMS threshold 0.01 and mean adjacent 2-Hz, 64 × 64 grayscale change threshold 2. 'Only' means only one metric crossed threshold.

072.title: Does louder sound predict a more changed endpoint?
072.caption: Of 7,242 clips in the highest RMS quarter, 1,991 also fall in the highest quarter for first-to-last frame difference. All 16 combinations occur.
072.scope: 28,969 eligible recordings from a 30,000-component candidate draw · first ten seconds
072.method: Use the original cached ten-second audio RMS and the mean absolute pixel difference between first and last sampled video frames. Make quartiles separately within the 28,969 eligible clips. Endpoint difference can miss internal movement.

073.title: Do the biggest sound and picture changes coincide?
073.caption: For 28 of 198 clips, the largest change in sound level and the largest change in visual activity occur at the same one-second boundary.
073.scope: 198 reserve clips with a unique largest jump in both profiles
073.method: Make ten RMS levels and ten within-second frame-change means (three internal transitions per second). Take the absolute first difference of each profile. Exclude ties for either largest jump. Bins show absolute separation; shared timing does not identify a shared event.

075.title: Compare cue seconds with their neighbours
075.caption: In 78 of 158 clips, seconds containing a subtitle onset have higher mean RMS than the other seconds in that same clip.
075.scope: 158 clips with both onset-bearing and onset-free seconds
075.method: Bin nonempty subtitle starts on the recording clock into one-second intervals. Subtract each clip’s mean RMS without an onset from its mean RMS with an onset. Multiple cues in a second count once. Speech may extend across bins.

076.title: Silent audio and identical endpoint frames
076.caption: Exactly 100 clips have zero decoded RMS. Of these, 97 still have different endpoint frames. Identical endpoints can hide changes in between.
076.scope: 28,969 eligible recordings from a 30,000-component candidate draw · first ten seconds
076.method: Count exact zeros in the original cached signal diagnostics. Endpoint equality means the first and last sampled frame arrays are equal; it does not test every frame in between.

077.title: An empty subtitle window can still be loud
077.caption: Of 5,186 clips with no subtitle onset, 4,928 have RMS at or above 0.01. The absence of a new line supplies little evidence of silence.
077.scope: 28,969 eligible recordings from a 30,000-component candidate draw · first ten seconds
077.method: Use exact stored subtitle-start counts and audio RMS from the same original ten-second extraction window. RMS reveals energy only; voice, music and environment have not been classified.

080.title: Three clocks on the same ten seconds
080.caption: Read down each recording. Sound energy, pixel change and subtitle onset times can peak at different moments. A missing tick means no new subtitle starts in that interval.
080.scope: Three selected recordings · common ten-second axis
080.method: Decode mono at 16 kHz; measure 100 consecutive 100-ms bins per clip. Sample video at 4 frames/s and resize to 96 × 64; luma = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B. Normalise envelope and change separately to the maximum within each record; ticks are original subtitle onsets relative to the stored clip start.

082.title: A train photograph and the approach to a platform
082.caption: The linked still already contains a train. The opening frame of the video gives rails and grass; a platform and carriage enter the later view. Its single subtitle onset is right at the start.
082.scope: One linked WIT image and recording · source offset 0:00 · first ten seconds of the stored clip
082.method: Hand-selected visual example. Frame labels are requested times from stored clip start. Tick marks show nonempty subtitle onsets within [source offset, source offset + 10 s). Cue ends are unknown.

main.title: What crosses a release split?

main.title: What can you hear when no subtitle starts?

appendix.title: How a recording enters a batch

items.note: Ten-window recordings account for 61.5% of recording IDs and 75.1% of stored rows.
Eight recordings have ten windows apiece. Their first-to-last spans range from 4.5 to 81 minutes.
Two saved search orderings agree on the first result for 22 of 62 historical collector queries.
Among 37,706 pairs of recordings linked to the same picture, 24,613 pairs have no title word in common.
Among WIT entries carrying Portuguese metadata, 57.9% also carry Spanish metadata. The denominator changes with the conditioning edition.
For 105,198 of 105,544 WIT entries, every observed main-image flag is true. The other entries have no usable flag.
The animal chapter yields candidate page links for 37 of 56 language-specific concepts. The other ten chapters have different inventories and denominators.
A recording about an Alpina car links to an Alpinia flower. A dinosaur recording links to a grasshopper. Both pairs illustrate a limit of title-based collection.
items.scope: Two deliberately chosen examples of weak links.

items.note: Starting the subtitle clock at zero changes whether a cue is counted for 10,544 of 45,333 sampled rows with a nonzero source offset.
The central quarter of the picture contains 31.8% of measured pixel change on average across 200 clips with measurable change.
Among 198 clips with a unique largest change in each signal, the largest sound and picture changes share a one-second boundary in 28.
Three recordings put sound energy, pixel change and subtitle starts on the same ten-second clock.
